newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond volatilities stay well bid.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond volatilities stay well bid.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. Treasury bond options were well bid in late trade as the underlying market shed early gains, dealers said.

"Volatilities are building up here a little bit," said a brokerage firm trader at the Chicago Board of Trade, noting that demand for options was underpinned by caution ahead of Friday's November U.S. employment report and concern that the market was overdue for a correction.
Implied volatilities for January and March T-bond futures options stood at 11.1 and 10.4 percent, little changed from Monday but up a few tenths of a point from early lows.

Although the bond market rallied in the morning, helped by weaker than expected October U.S. new home sales data, it came under pressure in the afternoon on news of International Business Machines Corp's $850 million 100-year debenture.
Still, while most traders anticipated a correction to the market's month-long rally, they expected the underlying trend in bonds to stay bullish.
The CBOT trader said that given the resilience the market has shown in recent intra-day pullbacks, option traders were still wary of the time-decay risk.
Indeed, volatilities were still fragile at the shorter end of the yield curve on sentiment that short-term interest rates would stay steady for a while.
Implied volatilities for March and June Eurodollar futures options stood at 10.7 and 14.8 percent respectively, off 0.2 and 0.5 percentage point.

"The (option) market just displays the front Euros' sluggishness -- we're going up but we're really not going anywhere," said a Eurodollar trader at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange. "It just makes people complacent.

"It seems like maybe these employment numbers are going to take less of a profile than they have taken in the past," he added. "If it's weak, the market will certainly rally, but if it's a strong number, it won't have much of an impact."
Order flows in Eurodollar options were moderate, with selling focusing on the shorter maturities.

"June puts seemed to be the thing to sell," the CME trader said. A U.S. bank affiliate sold 1,000 lots each of June 94.50 puts and September 94.25 puts in early trade, leading off a flurry of similar-sized selling in June puts, he noted.
